claim: Cortical networks exhibit intrinsic dynamics that drive coordinated, large-scale fluctuations across neuronal populations and create noise correlations that impact sensory coding.
source: Cortical networks exhibit intrinsic dynamics that drive coordinated, large-scale fluctuations across neuronal populations and create noise correlations that impact sensory coding.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general finding of the study, supported by the experimental recordings and modeling work presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The deterministic spiking network model generated correlated variability without external noise.
source: The model generated correlated variability without external noise and accurately reproduced the diverse activity patterns in our recordings.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through the model simulations shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Differences in noise correlations across recordings were due primarily to differences in the strength of feedback inhibition.
source: Analysis of the model parameters suggested that differences in noise correlations across recordings were due primarily to differences in the strength of feedback inhibition.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the analysis shown in Figure 5a, which shows that inhibition explains the most variance in noise correlations (r²=0.73, p<10⁻¹⁸).

claim: Putative inhibitory neurons were more active during desynchronized cortical states with weak noise correlations.
source: Further analysis of our recordings confirmed that putative inhibitory neurons were indeed more active during desynchronized cortical states with weak noise correlations.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 6, showing increased FS neuron activity during desynchronized states.

claim: Inhibition modulates the interactions between intrinsic dynamics and sensory inputs to control the strength of noise correlations.
source: Our results demonstrate that network models with intrinsically-generated variability can accurately reproduce the activity patterns observed in multi-neuron recordings and suggest that inhibition modulates the interactions between intrinsic dynamics and sensory inputs to control the strength of noise correlations.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, synthesizing the findings from the model and experimental analyses.

claim: Correlations between pairs of neurons are driven by dynamics involving coordinated, large-scale fluctuations in the activity of many cortical neurons.
source: The correlations between pairs of neurons have been studied extensively (Cohen and Kohn, 2011; Ecker et al., 2010; Averbeck et al., 2006), and recent studies have demonstrated that they are driven by dynamics involving coordinated, large-scale fluctuations in the activity of many cortical neurons (Sakata and Harris, 2009; Pachitariu et al., 2015; Okun et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Inactivation of the cortical circuit suppresses synchronized fluctuations at the level of the membrane potential in both awake and anesthetized animals.
source: Inactivation of the cortical circuit suppresses these synchronized fluctuations at the level of the membrane potential, in both awake and anesthetized animals, suggesting that this synchronization is cortical in origin (Cohen-Kashi Malina et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cohen-Kashi Malina et al., 2016.

claim: Various factors modulate the strength of correlations, including anesthesia, attention, locomotion, and alertness.
source: Importantly, the nature of these dynamics and the correlations that they create are dependent on the state of the underlying network; it has been shown that various factors modulate the strength of correlations, such as anesthesia (Harris and Thiele, 2011; Schölvinck et al., 2015; Constantinople and Bruno, 2011), attention (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Mitchell et al., 2009; Buran et al., 2014), locomotion (Schneider et al., 2014; Erisken et al., 2014), and alertness (Vinck et al., 2015; McGinley et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The standard assumption that correlations arise from common input noise does not provide insight into their genesis.
source: While a number of modeling studies have explored the impact of correlations on sensory coding (Shadlen et al., 1996; de la Rocha et al., 2007; Averbeck et al., 2006; Pillow et al., 2008; Ecker et al., 2011; Moreno-Bote et al., 2014), there have been few efforts to identify their biophysical origin; the standard assumption that correlations arise from common input noise (de la Rocha et al., 2007; Doiron et al., 2016; Lyamzin et al., 2015) simply pushes the correlations from spiking to the membrane voltage without providing insight into their genesis.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous modeling approaches, supported by citations.

claim: No external noise is needed to generate the correlated activity observed in vivo.
source: However, no external noise is needed to generate the correlated activity that is observed in vivo; in vitro experimental studies have shown that cortical networks are capable of generating large-scale fluctuations intrinsically (Sanchez-Vives et al., 2010; Sanchez-Vives and McCormick, 2000), and in vivo results suggest that the majority of cortical fluctuations arise locally (Cohen-Kashi Malina et al., 2016; Shapcott et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies showing intrinsic generation of fluctuations.

claim: The network model has five free parameters controlling excitatory connectivity strength, inhibitory feedback strength, adaptation strength, and tonic input.
source: The model has five free parameters: three controlling the average strength of excitatory connectivity, the strength of inhibitory feedback, and the strength of adaptation, respectively, and two controlling the strength of the tonic input to each neuron, which is chosen from an exponential distribution.
evidence: This is a direct description of the model structure.

claim: The timescales controlling decay of excitatory, inhibitory and adaptation currents are fixed at 5.10 ms, 3.75 ms and 375 ms, respectively.
source: The timescales that control the decay of the excitatory, inhibitory and adaptation currents are fixed at 5.10 ms, 3.75 ms and 375 ms, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct specification of model parameters.

claim: Population-wide fluctuations over hundreds of milliseconds are generated when slow adaptation currents synchronize across neurons.
source: Population-wide fluctuations over hundreds of milliseconds are generated when the slow adaptation currents synchronize across neurons to maintain a similar state of adaptation throughout the entire network, which, in turn, results in coordinated spiking (Latham et al., 2000; Destexhe, 2009).
evidence: This describes the mechanism by which the model generates fluctuations, supported by citations.

claim: A single spike added randomly to a single neuron during simulated activity is capable of changing the time course of large-scale fluctuations.
source: In fact, a single spike added randomly to a single neuron during simulated activity is capable of changing the time course of large-scale fluctuations, in some cases triggering immediate population-wide spiking (Figure 2b, top rows).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2b showing the effect of adding a single spike to the network.

claim: Similar phenomena of single-spike sensitivity have been observed in vivo previously.
source: Similar phenomena have been observed in vivo previously (London et al., 2010) and were also evident in our recordings when comparing different extracts of cortical activity; spike patterns that were similar for several seconds often then began to diverge almost immediately (Figure 2b, bottom rows).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and by data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Each of the five model parameters can exert strong control over the dynamics of the network.
source: The results of these parameter sweeps clearly demonstrate that each of the five parameters can exert strong control over the dynamics of the network, as both the overall level of activity and the spatial and temporal structure of the patterns in simulated activity varied widely with changes in each parameter (Figure 2c–d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the parameter sweep analysis shown in Figure 2c-d.

claim: The model was fit to 59 multi-neuron populations across six unique recording types.
source: We compiled recordings from a total of 59 multi-neuron populations across six unique recording types (i.e. species/modality/state combinations; see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the dataset used in the study.

claim: Large-scale fluctuations were weak in awake animals and strong under anesthesia in general, but this was not always the case.
source: In general, large-scale fluctuations were weak in awake animals and strong under anesthesia, but this was not always the case (see further examples in Figure 3 and summary statistics for each recording in Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: Three principal components were required to account for the differences in spike patterns across recordings.
source: This was confirmed by principal component analysis; even in the already reduced space described by our summary statistics, three principal components were required to account for the differences in spike patterns across recordings (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1e through principal component analysis.

claim: The model was flexible enough to capture the wide variety of activity patterns observed across recordings.
source: The model was flexible enough to capture the wide variety of activity patterns observed across our recordings, producing both decorrelated, tonic spiking and coordinated, large-scale fluctuations between up and down states as needed (see examples in Figure 3b, statistics for all recordings and models in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and parameter values and goodness-of-fit measures for all recordings in Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model fits shown in Figure 3 and supplementary figures.

claim: The median variance explained by the model of the autocorrelation function of the MUA, the distribution of MUA values across time bins, and the mean pairwise correlations were 82%, 90%, and 97% respectively.
source: We found that the median variance explained by the model of the autocorrelation function of the MUA, the distribution of MUA values across time bins, and the mean pairwise correlations were 82%, 90%, and 97% respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This quantifies the goodness of fit of the model, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3b.

claim: The noise correlations in the simulated cortical responses were similar to those in the recordings.
source: Using the subset of our cortical recordings in which we presented the same sounds that were also presented during the IC recordings, we verified that the noise correlations in the simulated cortical responses were similar to those in the recordings (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4e comparing model and recorded noise correlations.

claim: The amount of variance in noise correlations explained by the strength of inhibitory feedback was by far the largest compared to other parameters.
source: While several parameters were able to explain a significant amount of the variance in noise correlations across recordings, the amount of variance explained by the strength of inhibitory feedback was by far the largest (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5a, where inhibition has r²=0.73 compared to much lower values for other parameters.

claim: The predominance of inhibition in the control of noise correlations was confirmed by the measurement of partial correlations.
source: The predominance of inhibition in the control of noise correlations was confirmed by the measurement of partial correlations (the correlation between the noise correlations and each parameter that remains after factoring out the influence of the other parameters; partial r2 for inhibition: 0.67, excitation: 0.02, adaptation: 0.08, tonic input spread: 0.17, and tonic input baseline: 0.04).
evidence: This provides statistical evidence for the unique role of inhibition using partial correlation analysis.

claim: More than 90% of FS cortical neurons have been reported to be parvalbumin-positive (PV+) inhibitory neurons.
source: In general, more than 90% of FS cortical neurons have been reported to be parvalbumin-positive (PV+) inhibitory neurons (Nowak et al., 2003; Kawaguchi and Kubota, 1997; Barthó et al., 2004; Cho et al., 2010; Madisen et al., 2012; Stark et al., 2013; Cohen and Mizrahi, 2015), and this value approaches 100% in the deep cortical layers where we recorded (Cardin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: There was a four-fold increase in the mean spike rate of FS neurons from the most synchronized trials to the most desynchronized trials, while RS activity remained constant.
source: As predicted by our model-based analyses, the change in noise correlations with cortical synchrony was accompanied by a change in FS activity; there was a four-fold increase in the mean spike rate of FS neurons from the most synchronized trials to the most desynchronized trials, while RS activity remained constant (Figure 6d–f).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6d-f for awake mouse recordings.

claim: Cortical desynchronization under urethane was accompanied by a decrease in noise correlations and an increase in FS activity.
source: As in our awake recordings, cortical desynchronization under urethane was accompanied by a decrease in noise correlations and an increase in FS activity (Figure 6h–k).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6h-k for urethane recordings.

claim: Both FS and RS activity increased with cortical desynchronization under urethane, but the increase in FS activity was much larger (110% and 42%, respectively).
source: In fact, both FS and RS activity increased with cortical desynchronization under urethane, but the increase in FS activity was much larger (110% and 42%, respectively).
evidence: This quantifies the differential changes in FS and RS activity under urethane.

claim: The model captured the change in dynamics associated with running through an increase in inhibition and a decrease in adaptation in all four recordings.
source: In all four recordings, the model captured the change in dynamics associated with running through an increase in inhibition and a decrease in adaptation (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7d for locomotion recordings.

claim: Although both FS and RS populations increased their activity during running, the relative increase in FS activity was significantly larger.
source: Although both FS and RS populations increased their activity during running, the relative increase in FS activity was significantly larger (Figure 7e; on average, FS activity increased by 87% and RS activity increased by 28%).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7e with statistical significance indicated.

claim: No previous models have been able to reproduce large-scale coordinated activity in a deterministic network of connected neurons.
source: However, no previous models have been able to reproduce such large-scale coordinated activity in a deterministic network of connected neurons; previous models only reproduced single-neuron variability (Vogels and Abbott, 2005; Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2012).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous modeling work, supported by citations.

claim: Networks in the classical balanced state produce activity with zero mean pairwise correlations between neurons.
source: Networks in the classical balanced state produce activity with zero mean pairwise correlations between neurons (Doiron et al., 2016; van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1996; Renart et al., 2010) and, thus, are not suitable to describe the population-wide fluctuations that are observed in many brain states in vivo (Okun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about previous models, supported by citations.

claim: Clustered networks produce activity with positive correlations between a small fraction of neuron pairs (less than 1 in 1000), but the average noise correlations across all pairs are still near zero.
source: However, while clustered networks do produce activity with positive correlations between a small fraction of neuron pairs (less than 1 in 1000), the average noise correlations across all pairs are still near zero and, thus, these networks are still unable to generate population-wide fluctuations.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of clustered network models.

claim: The population-wide fluctuations generated by the interaction between recurrent excitation and adaptation were a robust feature of the network and persisted in more sophisticated networks.
source: The population-wide fluctuations generated by the interaction between recurrent excitation and adaptation were a robust feature of the network and persisted in more sophisticated networks that included multiple conductance timescales, many more neurons, spiking inhibitory neurons, structured connectivity, and kurtotic distributions of synaptic efficacies (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: When inhibition is weak, small deviations from the mean spike rate can be amplified by strong, non-specific, recurrent excitation into population-wide events (up states).
source: When inhibition is weak, small deviations from the mean spike rate can be amplified by strong, non-specific, recurrent excitation into population-wide events (up states).
evidence: This describes the mechanism by which weak inhibition leads to large-scale fluctuations.

claim: External inputs arriving shortly after an up state will generally result in many fewer spikes than those arriving during a down state.
source: The intrinsic temporal variability in the network imposes a history dependence on evoked responses; because of the build-up of adaptation currents during each spiking event, external inputs arriving shortly after an up state will generally result in many fewer spikes than those arriving during a down state (Curto et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes how history dependence creates noise correlations, supported by a citation.

claim: Strong inhibition can sharpen tuning in a network without any structured connectivity simply by controlling its dynamics.
source: Our results, however, demonstrate that strong inhibition can sharpen tuning in a network without any structured connectivity simply by controlling its dynamics.
evidence: This is a key finding about the mechanism of tuning sharpening.

claim: When inhibition is weak, every external input will eventually excite every neuron in the network because those neurons that receive the input directly will relay indirect excitation to the rest of the network.
source: In our model, broad tuning curves result from the over-excitability of the network. When inhibition is weak, every external input will eventually excite every neuron in the network because those neurons that receive the input directly will relay indirect excitation to the rest of the network.
evidence: This describes the mechanism by which weak inhibition leads to broad tuning.

claim: Locomotion in particular tends to depolarize cortical neurons, and in some cases increases tonic spiking.
source: Locomotion in particular tends to depolarizate cortical neurons, and in some cases increases tonic spiking (Niell and Stryker, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Niell and Stryker, 2010.

claim: Task-engagement in stationary animals has been associated with hyperpolarization and suppression of activity.
source: In contrast, task-engagement in stationary animals has been associated with hyperpolarization and suppression of activity (McGinley et al., 2015a; Otazu et al., 2009; Buran et al., 2014) (but not all studies find a decrease in membrane potential during task engagement [Sachidhanandam et al., 2013]).
evidence: This is supported by citations, with a caveat about conflicting findings.

claim: In vitro studies have shown that pharmacologically reducing inhibition increases the strength of the correlations between excitatory neurons in a graded manner.
source: In vitro studies have shown that pharmacologically reducing inhibition increases the strength of the correlations between excitatory neurons in a graded manner (Sippy and Yuste, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sippy and Yuste, 2013.

claim: In vivo whole-cell recordings in awake animals have demonstrated that the stimulus-evoked inhibitory conductance, measured at the soma, is much larger than the corresponding excitatory conductance.
source: In vivo whole-cell recordings in awake animals have demonstrated that the stimulus-evoked inhibitory conductance, measured at the soma, is much larger than the corresponding excitatory conductance (Haider et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Haider et al., 2013.

claim: This strong inhibition in awake animals quickly shunts the excitatory drive and results in sharper tuning and sparser firing than the balanced excitatory and inhibitory conductances observed under anesthesia.
source: This strong inhibition in awake animals quickly shunts the excitatory drive and results in sharper tuning and sparser firing than the balanced excitatory and inhibitory conductances observed under anesthesia (Wehr and Zador, 2003; Haider et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wehr and Zador, 2003 and Haider et al., 2013.

claim: Several studies have found an increase in putative parvalbumin-positive (PV+) inhibitory neuron firing during running.
source: There is controversy in the literature as to whether somatostatin-positive (SOM+) inhibitory neurons increase their activity during running, but several studies have found an increase in putative parvalbumin-positive (PV+) inhibitory neuron firing during running (Niell and Stryker, 2010; Polack et al., 2013; Vinck et al., 2015; Pakan et al., 2016), consistent with our results.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The activation of inhibitory interneurons generally results in sharper tuning, weaker correlations, and enhanced behavioral performance.
source: While the exact roles played by different inhibitory neuron types are still under investigation (Lee et al., 2014; Seybold et al., 2015), the activation of inhibitory interneurons generally results in sharper tuning, weaker correlations, and enhanced behavioral performance (Wilson et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2015), while suppression of inhibitory interneurons has the opposite effect, decreasing the signal-to-noise ratio and reliability of evoked responses across trials (Zhu et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to optogenetic studies.

claim: One recent study found that the best performance in a detection task was observed on trials in which the pre-stimulus membrane voltage was hyperpolarized and low-frequency fluctuations were absent.
source: In fact, one recent study found that the best performance in a detection task was observed on trials in which the pre-stimulus membrane voltage was hyperpolarized and low-frequency fluctuations were absent (McGinley et al., 2015a), consistent with a suppressed, inhibition-stabilized network state.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McGinley et al., 2015a.

claim: Increases in acetylcholine (ACh) and norepinephrine (NE) have been observed during wakefulness and arousal.
source: Increases in acetylcholine (ACh) and norepinephrine (NE) have been observed during wakefulness and arousal (Berridge and Waterhouse, 2003; Jones, 2008), and during periods of cortical desynchronization in which slow fluctuations in the LFP are suppressed (Goard and Dan, 2009; Chen et al., 2015; Castro-Alamancos and Gulati, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Stimulation of the basal forebrain has been shown to produce ACh-mediated increases in the activity of FS neurons and decrease the variability of evoked responses in cortex.
source: Stimulation of the basal forebrain has been shown to produce ACh-mediated increases in the activity of FS neurons and decrease the variability of evoked responses in cortex (Sakata, 2016; Castro-Alamancos and Gulati, 2014; Goard and Dan, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Optogenetic activation of cholinergic projections to cortex resulted in increased firing of SOM+ inhibitory neurons and reduced slow fluctuations.
source: In addition, optogenetic activation of cholinergic projections to cortex resulted in increased firing of SOM+ inhibitory neurons and reduced slow fluctuations (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2015.

claim: The release of NE in cortex through microdialysis had similar effects, increasing fast-spiking activity and reducing spontaneous spike rates.
source: The release of NE in cortex through microdialysis had similar effects, increasing fast-spiking activity and reducing spontaneous spike rates (Castro-Alamancos and Gulati, 2014), while blocking NE receptors strengthened slow fluctuations in membrane potential (Constantinople and Bruno, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Castro-Alamancos and Gulati, 2014 and Constantinople and Bruno, 2011.

claim: The network simulations ran 10000x faster than real time using GPU computing.
source: By using GPU computing resources, we were able to design and implement network simulations that ran 10000x faster than real time, making it feasible to sample the cost function with high resolution and locate its global minimum to identify the parameter configuration that resulted in activity patterns that best matched those of each recording.
evidence: This describes the computational methods used.

claim: The neurons in the model network are connected randomly and sparsely with 5% probability.
source: Each neuron receives constant tonic input, and the neurons are connected randomly and sparsely with 5% probability.
evidence: This is a specification of the model architecture.

claim: The supralinearity of the inhibitory feedback is a critical feature of the network.
source: The supralinearity of the inhibitory feedback is a critical feature of the network, as it shifts the balance of excitation and inhibition in favor of inhibition when the network is strongly driven, as has been observed in awake animals (Haider et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes a key feature of the model, supported by a citation.

claim: Approximately one million networks were simulated on a grid of parameters for 900 s each of spontaneous activity.
source: Approximately one million networks were simulated on a grid of parameters for 900 s each of spontaneous activity, and their summary statistics (cθ,MUAθ and ACFθ) were retained.
evidence: This describes the computational approach used for model fitting.

claim: The Fano factors of the responses of IC neurons are close to one and the noise correlations between neurons are extremely weak.
source: We have shown previously that the Fano factors of the responses of IC neurons are close to one and the noise correlations between neurons are extremely weak (Garcia-Lazaro et al., 2013), suggesting that the spiking activity of a population of IC neurons can be well described by series of independent, inhomogeneous Poisson processes.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Garcia-Lazaro et al., 2013.

claim: Noise correlations were generally stronger during synchronized trials than during desynchronized trials in awake mice.
source: As expected, noise correlations were generally stronger during synchronized trials than during desynchronized trials, and this variation in noise correlations with cortical synchrony was evident both within individual recordings and across animals (Figure 6b–c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6b-c for awake mouse recordings.

claim: The increase in RS activity during running despite increased FS activity is likely due to an accompanying decrease in adaptation.
source: Our results suggest that the increase in RS activity during running despite increased FS activity is likely due to an accompanying decrease in adaptation.
evidence: This is an inference from the model fitting results for locomotion.

claim: The cortical desynchronization under urethane may involve other mechanisms in addition to an increase in feedback inhibition.
source: The increase in RS activity suggests that cortical desynchronization under urethane may involve other mechanisms in addition to an increase in feedback inhibition (a comparison of the model parameters fit to desynchronized and synchronized urethane recordings (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) suggests that the average level of tonic input is significantly higher during desynchronization (desynchronized: 0.075 ± 0.008, synchronized: 0.0195 ± 0.0054, p=0.006)).
evidence: This is an inference from the parameter fits and statistical comparison.

claim: The onset of a stimulus quenches variability and switches the cortex from a synchronized to a desynchronized state.
source: This increase in the inhibitory gain of the driven network provides a possible mechanistic explanation for the recent observation that the onset of a stimulus quenches variability (Churchland et al., 2010) and switches the cortex from a synchronized to a desynchronized state (Tan et al., 2014), as well as for the suppression of responses to high-contrast stimuli in alert animals (Zhuang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model results in the context of previous experimental findings, supported by citations.
